UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                               BEFORE THE
                           FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                           )
Maryland Office of People’s Counsel                        )

v.                                                                                   Docket No. EL26-63
                                                           )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                )

             COMMENTS OF THE NEW JERSEY BOARD OF PUBLIC UTILITIES
           Pursuant to Rule 213,1 the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (“NJBPU” or “Board”) hereby

submits the following comments in support of the Complaint2 filed by the Maryland Office of People’s

Council (“MD OPC”). The Complaint asserts that PJM’s regional transmission cost-allocation

methodology is no longer appropriate under the new paradigm in which concentrated and discrete large-

load additions are the main drivers of transmission investment.3 Under this paradigm, New Jersey

ratepayers, like Maryland ratepayers, are allocated high transmission costs for load growth primarily

located outside of the state. The Board agrees it is appropriate and necessary, under the cost causation

principle, to revisit PJM’s current cost allocation methods given the changed circumstances driving future

transmission needs.


     I.    Data Centers are Creating the Need for New Infrastructure and Costs are Being
           Inappropriately Socialized Across Existing Ratepayers
           Historically high projections of large load development, mainly driven by data centers, have had

significant impacts on New Jersey ratepayers and the entire PJM region. Most notably, in the 2025/26

 delivery year, the PJM capacity market saw a massive jump in its clearing price, largely driven by rapid

demand growth from data centers which contributed to a tightening supply-demand balance. This led to

New Jersey ratepayers experiencing an average monthly bill increase between 17.23% and 20.20%.4

Similar bill increases were seen across the PJM region. In response, the Commission approved a price

collar for the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 delivery years,5 which was subsequently extended for two

additional delivery years.6 This short-term solution was necessary to protect ratepayers, but it did not

resolve the instigating cause – unprecedented data center load growth and the costs being imposed across

the system.


           In this context, PJM ran a stakeholder process to discuss how to implement a Reliability Backstop

Procurement for new capacity, as well as a Connect and Manage framework to address the impacts of a

capacity shortfall. Through the process, stakeholders recognized that data centers should be paying for

the infrastructure and resultant system-wide costs they cause. For instance, the January 16, 2026,

Statement of Principles on PJM from the White House and 13 PJM Governors stated that the costs of new

capacity should be correspondingly allocated to data centers.7 The Board’s President submitted a letter to

PJM on March 27, 2026, explaining that Connect and Manage load should be removed from the capacity

market to ensure existing customers do not “pay for new generation needs caused by the influx of new

large load additions such as data centers.”8 A group of state legislators similarly called upon PJM to

remove large loads from the capacity market demand stack until the data centers have brought new supply

to the system to offset their load.9 Together, these statements underscore broad agreement that the costs

 to serve data center load should not be socialized across existing ratepayers. Rather, data centers should

bear the costs of the new generation needed to serve them.


            This argument naturally extends to transmission cost allocation. Data centers, not existing

ratepayers, should pay for the cost of the significant new transmission infrastructure that will be needed to

serve them. The Commission itself recognized the data center impact on transmission planning through

its June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause, preliminarily finding that PJM’s tariff appears to be unjust and

unreasonable because network upgrade interconnection costs may be “shift[ed]” from data centers to

other transmission customers.10 The Board commends the Commission for its actions while noting that

the Order does not appear to address the specific issue of baseline transmission upgrade cost allocation

raised in the Complaint.


            The Commission is the only entity able to adequately address the improper allocation of data

center-related regional transmission costs. As the Commission itself explained, “[w]ith respect to the

addition of large loads to the transmission system, the Commission has exclusive authority to ensure that

transmission rates are just and reasonable.”11 This authority extends to all Commission-jurisdictional

transmission, not just the Network Upgrades which are specifically identified through large load

interconnection requests. State regulators cannot ensure just and reasonable retail rates if the zones within

their jurisdiction are assigned costs driven by out-of-state loads that are not subject to their jurisdiction.


            PJM and the Commission have conducted proceedings to implement various market and planning

reforms, but as reflected by the Complaint, ongoing work remains to be done at the regional level. The

Complaint presents another instance where data centers are causing system cost increases that tend to be

socialized across existing ratepayers throughout the region. However, the broader problem of the effects

of data centers’ impact on ratepayers should not be resolved based upon an isolated example of the

                                                         3
 problem or on a state-by-state basis. Such an approach would disregard the reality that regional

projections of data center load in the aggregate have directly impacted regional capacity market and

energy prices and regional transmission investment needs. Regional solutions in all these areas must be

implemented in coordination with one another to ensure existing ratepayers are protected from every area

which has been upended by the unprecedented rate of data center load growth.


     II.   New Jersey is Similarly Impacted Due to the Current Cost Allocation Methodology

           The Complaint describes how Maryland ratepayers are assigned $2.0 billion in capital costs

across three successive Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) cycles “for transmission

infrastructure driven overwhelmingly by data center load growth occurring outside Maryland’s

borders.”12 New Jersey is similarly impacted.


           The PJM region required significant infrastructure investment to reliably serve a huge increase in

expected load growth in the 2025 RTEP Window 1, with transmission infrastructure investments totaling

an estimated $11.8 billion.13 Board staff has calculated the capital costs assigned to Atlantic City Electric,

(“ACE”), Jersey Central Power and Light (“JCPL”), Public Service Electric & Gas (“PSE&G”), and

Rockland Electric Company (“RECO”) (cumulatively “New Jersey zones”) from the 2025 RTEP Window

1 by applying PJM’s 50%LRS/50% DFAX cost allocation methodology to the estimated costs of each

regional project, and applying PJM’s 100% DFAX cost allocation methodology to each non-regional

project approved in that window.14 Of the $11.8 billion in capital costs, New Jersey ratepayers have been

 allocated $1.12 billion across all four New Jersey zones.15 Of that total, $517 million is due to the load-

ratio-share component of regionally allocated lines. Yet comparison of the 2024 load forecast to the 2025

load forecast used to identify the need for these lines actually showed a decrease in summer and winter

peak load expected for all New Jersey zones, except PSE&G, up to 2035.16 Load growth for most New

Jersey zones was already taken into account and planned for in the 2024 RTEP Window 1. The cost of

regional infrastructure built to address increasing load is therefore completely disproportionate to the

contributions of each of the New Jersey zones to its need. As a result, New Jersey ratepayers are being

assigned costs that they have not caused or derived a comparable benefit from.


             Atlantic City Electric, for example, is forecasted to have a summer and winter peak growth rate of

0.1% and 2.4%, respectively, for 2035.17 Winter peak is only expected to grow by 437 MW in a ten-year

timeframe.18 Yet under PJM’s cost allocation methodology, ACE is assigned $71.3 million in capital

costs through the load-ratio-share portion of the allocation alone.19 This proportion of costs is

unsustainable and is a clear example of New Jersey customers subsidizing infrastructure mainly caused by

data centers.


             By these comments, the Board is not saying that all costs assigned to New Jersey ratepayers in the

2025 RTEP Window 1, and future RTEPs, are unjust and unreasonable. Nor does the Board suggest the

Commission should revisit cost allocations or the cost allocation methods for transmission projects

 planned before the recent influx of significant data center load growth. However, when applied to the

new phenomenon of very large loads from a single industry creating unprecedented forecast error and

stranded asset risk, the cost allocation status quo results in a level of socialization that is incompatible

with the cost-causation principle. It also undermines retail regulators’ ability to assign the true costs of

managing those risks to the economic actors that are causing them. This leaves existing ratepayers

holding the bag for billions of dollars in transmission costs, some of which may ultimately prove

unnecessary, caused by a single industry that does not have to bear the full cost of its private business

decisions.


III.       Revisiting the Existing Cost Allocation Methodology is Appropriate Given
           Infrastructure is Mainly Driven by Geographically Concentrated, Large Load
           Growth.
       Under the cost causation principle, the rates charged for electricity should reflect the costs of

providing it and ensure that the “burden is matched with benefit.”20 Data centers are both the greatest

causers and the beneficiaries of most current regionally-planned transmission, as they are the main drivers

of the load growth which transmission investment is intended to solve. While the Board recognizes New

Jersey ratepayers may still receive ancillary benefits from regional lines, it is incumbent upon the

Commission to establish cost allocation rules which reflect this new reality, as the Commission “is not

authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its

members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its

members."21 The Board agrees with the MD OPC’s conclusion that “when the driver of transmission

investment is concentrated large load growth in a discrete geographic area, the rationale for the load-ratio-

share component of PJM’s hybrid methodology fails.”22 Under the new paradigm in which load growth is

no longer approximately even over the zones, and where that load growth can be so clearly tied to a single

                                                         6
 class of customers concentrated in discrete geographical areas, a load ratio share approach based on

existing load may no longer be appropriate. The Board encourages the exploration of other cost

allocation methodologies which may lead to just and reasonable rates. While the Board does not opine on

any specific solution at this time, it stands ready to engage and explore various alternatives. The

Commission should direct PJM and the relevant transmission owners to explore more equitable cost

distributions to reflect the new realities of localized large load growth.


IV.     Conclusion

        Unprecedented and geographically constrained load growth, mainly attributed to data centers, has

caused significant need for reforms in all areas of the PJM markets and planning processes. The MD

OPC Complaint highlights another instance where reform is necessary, as the costs of baseline

transmission infrastructure meant to address this load growth are being improperly socialized to other

ratepayers in both Maryland and New Jersey. The Commission is the appropriate entity to address the

unjust and unreasonable cost shifting, and it should direct PJM and the relevant transmission owners to

explore other cost allocation methodologies.


Respectfully submitted,
